newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Labour would review inflation measure.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Labour would review inflation measure.

text.p: Labour Party Finance spokesman Michael Cullen said on Thursday a Labour government would change the Reserve Bank's inflation target to -1-3 percent from 0-2 percent, but only as a holding action ahead of a review of how to measure inflation.
He told a news briefing a review would take six to 12 months. He said the 0-2 percent inflation target was "clearly too tight".
"We are not building in a change in the mid-point," he said.

"That's only a holding action while we review how to measure inflation. We are not convinced it (the Reserve Bank's method of measuring underlying inflation) is the best measure," he said in answer to questions.
Cullen said Labour's fiscal projections adopted Treasury's growth projections and it had not built in any change to growth from the impact of its policies which were "likely to be self-balancing".
"There is no reason any party should use figures other than Treasury's forecasts," he said, adding that was the only way different parties' policies could be compared.

He said Labour had earlier committed to a bottom line on net debt reduction rather than a level of fiscal surplus. That bottom line was to reduce by an average of two percent net debt as a percentage of GDP for each of the next three years.
Longer term, he expected government revenues to stabilise about 35 percent of GDP and spending around 34 percent, with the bulk of the operating balance being dedicated to a superannuation fund.

He said the balance in the superannuation fund meant that while Labour's fiscal position was initially looser, "we are committed to a slightly tighter stance in the long term potentially than are National".
Labour was not "wedded to a figure of 20 percent of GDP" as a measure of prudent debt levels, Cullen said, adding that at 21.8 percent by the year 2000 "we are into the prudent level of debt".
In answer to questioning Cullen said he personally believed the exchange rate would drop "under almost any scenario".
He would not be drawn on the level of expenditure or fiscal balance he would consider prudent and therefore a bottom line in coalition talks.
